messages.subject: Interpreting variograms - single peak
parts:
I am analyzing multi-year data collected with VHF telemetry typically on a weekly basis. In most cases, the full data set (up to 8 years) reaches an asymptote (usually with some periodicity), but clearly indicating range residence, as shown in "F#1 variogram_all" and F#1 variogram_all_zoom." In 10 of 11 individuals examined so far, the best movement model has been the OU anisotropic model, although <3 dAICc better than the OUF anisotropic model (which was best in the remaining case). The IID model differs by 117-724 dAICc, so far.

I am also interested in annual home ranges, but with these data sub-sets, the variograms for the single-year data generally have a single peak before declining at longer lags, rather than approaching or fluctuating around an asymtptote (see "F#1 variogram_2003" and "F#1 variogram_2003zoom"). Nonetheless, model selection usually still results in the OU anisotropic model on top by similarly narrow margins, although the OUF anisotropic and IID anisotropic models sometimes come out on top by <2 dAICc or so. Is there a different interpretation for variograms like this, and should I be concerned about estimates from these models?

Thanks,
Roy

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Interpreting variograms - single peak
parts:
Hi Roy,

The 1st and 3rd variograms that show many years and 1 year look very much like you have a regular annual migration or shift. You can probably subset the winter/summer data to obtain a winter/summer range with asymptotically flat variograms denoting range residence. In principle, you can also calculate the average annual range, but the final pieces of this are not finished in the package. I believe I might have the model selection working for periodicities: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/periodogram.html (AIC/BIC do not work!) but I still have to make some changes to the home-range estimation code for these models, which will be its own paper.

OU and OUF are nested models that differ by 1 parameter. When OUF fails to outperform OU, it just reduces to OU with the same likelihood and so their AICc difference will be only ~2 in that case.

Best,
Chris

parts:
Hi Roy,

So the basic OUF/OU/IID family of models are all range-resident and stationary. If there is some type of range shift or expansion/contraction, then for these models you have to partition the data into consistent segments where the models are valid, like the winter hibernaculum for example. AKDE is general but movement models are not. More models are in production to make this easier, like the periodic models in the vignette.

As an aside, I don't know what your VHF data are like, but my experience with estimating turtle movement with GPS data is that calibrating the error beforehand is important to reduce resulting biases (overestimated distances). The uere() and uere()<- methods in the development branch on GitHub are pretty easy to use now, I think.

If the "Annual" dataset avoids the non-stationary caused by hibernation, then that would be good for the stationary models.

The nesting of the models is best described here: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1574954117301115 in figure 1.

You should apply the best movement model to each individual. The best model is determined by both sampling quality and movement behavior, so fixing the best model across individuals only makes sense if sampling quality and movement behavior is fixed across individuals, which will never happen except in simulation.

If you see the same peak in both the movement data's periodogram and the sampling schedule's periodogram, then there could be a real periodicity or an artifactual one. Model selection would have to be used to determine this case.

The periodicities are sharp peaks, whose width (if any) would mostly be given by the frequency resolution of the data. See here for more help with interpretation: https://movementecologyjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s40462-016-0084-7 but note that periodograms require a lot of data to look good. I will put this reference in the beginning of the vignette.

Best,
Chris

parts:
Hi Roy,

Regarding model selection between OUF & IOU (or, analogously, OU & BM), in earlier papers we though that it would be possible to apply conventional model selection, as these are nested models that only differ by 3 parameters (2D mean + tau_position). In short, that doesn't seem possible and the AIC values reported for the models here aren't really comparable, which is why we do not include IOU (or BM) in ctmm.select. There is a short note in the help file: The IOU & BM processes are only conditionally stationary and do not have a joint likelihood function L(data), but only a conditional likelihood function L(data|prior). If you try to take the limit of OUF->IOU or OU->BM, the joint likelihoods L(data) of the limiting IOU/BM processes diverge. On the other hand, if you just compare conditional likelihoods, with priors taken from the joint likelihood evaluation, then the conditional likelihood ratios don't seem to show any correspondence to the truth.

So we don't have a formal model selection procedure to say that #14 is not resident, but the empirical variogram and tau_position estimate certainly support that conclusion.

summary doesn't return anything on the BM process, because it doesn't have any of the simpler metrics (IMO). It just has a diffusion parameter, which is variance from an initial point per unit time.

The first #58 set looks absurdly good to me. The uncertainty on the empirical variogram is larger than the uncertainty on the model fit here. What's important is that one is inside the other most of the time and the model fit looks to be running right through the CIs of the empirical variogram.
I assume the second "allfit" #58 set includes the hibernaculum? This would violate the stationary model assumptions and could be causing the moderate discrepancy here.

One thing that can help with irregularly sampled data is fast=FALSE in variogram. This doesn't impact the model fit, but the empirical variogram will be less biased by sampling variation. Sometimes this explains short lag discrepancies as well.

For #1, the time averaging property of stationary variograms & likelihoods only works well if there are many of these events being averaged over. 8 times is not that much and would probably result in some upwards bias of the HR area estimate, as AKDE is not coded for periodicities yet. I would recommend segmenting winter/summer and checking that those variograms are flat before proceeding with them.

Best,
Chris

The "allfit" variograms with the green shading are the resultant fitted SVFs for the top model (OU). For #1, I should steer away from including all the hibernation observations in the full dataset, but I am still interested in looking at longer-term, cumulative space-use patterns. For the annual movement/space-use analyses, I do exclude all the repeat records during hibernation (i.e., I start the yearly dataset with the last observation in its hibernaculum and end with the first observation in the next hibernaculum, thereby encompassing the full activity season). Clearly, this is not a BM or IOU pattern over the season, but are there problems using the stationary models for inference with this pattern? Do I need to include certain caveats in inferences drawn from that kind of pattern? 

Just as an aside, a few tortoises add another complication to the hibernation issue by also going into dormancy in the heat of summer. I'll look into that issue once I feel like I've got a solid grasp on the hibernation end of things!

Hi Roy,

Regarding model selection between OUF & IOU (or, analogously, OU & BM), in earlier papers we though that it would be possible to apply conventional model selection, as these are nested models that only differ by 3 parameters (2D mean + tau_position). In short, that doesn't seem possible and the AIC values reported for the models here aren't really comparable, which is why we do not include IOU (or BM) in ctmm.select. There is a short note in the help file: The IOU & BM processes are only conditionally stationary and do not have a joint likelihood function L(data), but only a conditional likelihood function L(data|prior). If you try to take the limit of OUF->IOU or OU->BM, the joint likelihoods L(data) of the limiting IOU/BM processes diverge. On the other hand, if you just compare conditional likelihoods, with priors taken from the joint likelihood evaluation, then the conditional likelihood ratios don't seem to show any correspondence to the truth.

So we don't have a formal model selection procedure to say that #14 is not resident, but the empirical variogram and tau_position estimate certainly support that conclusion.

summary doesn't return anything on the BM process, because it doesn't have any of the simpler metrics (IMO). It just has a diffusion parameter, which is variance from an initial point per unit time.

Chris

Hi Roy,

Regarding model selection between OUF & IOU (or, analogously, OU & BM), in earlier papers we though that it would be possible to apply conventional model selection, as these are nested models that only differ by 3 parameters (2D mean + tau_position). In short, that doesn't seem possible and the AIC values reported for the models here aren't really comparable, which is why we do not include IOU (or BM) in ctmm.select. There is a short note in the help file: The IOU & BM processes are only conditionally stationary and do not have a joint likelihood function L(data), but only a conditional likelihood function L(data|prior). If you try to take the limit of OUF->IOU or OU->BM, the joint likelihoods L(data) of the limiting IOU/BM processes diverge. On the other hand, if you just compare conditional likelihoods, with priors taken from the joint likelihood evaluation, then the conditional likelihood ratios don't seem to show any correspondence to the truth.

So we don't have a formal model selection procedure to say that #14 is not resident, but the empirical variogram and tau_position estimate certainly support that conclusion.

summary doesn't return anything on the BM process, because it doesn't have any of the simpler metrics (IMO). It just has a diffusion parameter, which is variance from an initial point per unit time.

The first #58 set looks absurdly good to me. The uncertainty on the empirical variogram is larger than the uncertainty on the model fit here. What's important is that one is inside the other most of the time and the model fit looks to be running right through the CIs of the empirical variogram.
I assume the second "allfit" #58 set includes the hibernaculum? This would violate the stationary model assumptions and could be causing the moderate discrepancy here.

One thing that can help with irregularly sampled data is fast=FALSE in variogram. This doesn't impact the model fit, but the empirical variogram will be less biased by sampling variation. Sometimes this explains short lag discrepancies as well.

For #1, the time averaging property of stationary variograms & likelihoods only works well if there are many of these events being averaged over. 8 times is not that much and would probably result in some upwards bias of the HR area estimate, as AKDE is not coded for periodicities yet. I would recommend segmenting winter/summer and checking that those variograms are flat before proceeding with them.
